prompt: $16$ progamers are playing in a single elimination tournament. Each player has a different skill level and when two play against each other the one with the higher skill level will always win. Each round, each progamer plays a match against another and the loser is eliminated. This continues until only one remains. How many different progamers can reach the round that has $2$ players remaining?

solutions.title: Bound and construction
solutions.body:
A finalist wins the bracket half containing him, which has $8$ players, so he is better than the other $7$ players of his half. Hence at least $7$ players are weaker than every finalist, and the $7$ weakest players can never reach the final: at most $16-7=9$ players can.

Every one of the $9$ best can do it: put that player in one half of the bracket together with the $7$ weakest players, and put the other $8$ of the top $9$ in the other half. He is the best in his half, so he wins it and reaches the final. The answer is $9$.

**Answer: 9**

prompt: $16$ progamers are playing in another single elimination tournament. Each round, each of the remaining progamers plays against another and the loser is eliminated. Additionally, each time a progamer wins, he will have a ceremony to celebrate. A player's first ceremony is ten seconds long, and afterward each ceremony is ten seconds longer than the last. What is the total length in seconds of all the ceremonies over the entire tournament?

solutions.title: Sum by rounds
solutions.body:
In round $k$ ($k=1,2,3,4$) there are $8,4,2,1$ winners, and each has his $k$th ceremony of $10k$ seconds. Total: $8\cdot10+4\cdot20+2\cdot30+1\cdot40=80+80+60+40=260$ seconds.

**Answer: 260**

prompt: Dragoons take up $1\times1$ squares in the plane with sides parallel to the coordinate axes such that the interiors of the squares do not intersect. A dragoon can fire at another dragoon if the difference in the $x$-coordinates of their centers and the difference in the $y$-coordinates of their centers are both at most $6$, regardless of any dragoons in between. For example, a dragoon centered at $(4,5)$ can fire at a dragoon centered at the origin, but a dragoon centered at $(7,0)$ can not. A dragoon cannot fire at itself. What is the maximum number of dragoons that can fire at a single dragoon simultaneously?

solutions.title: Area bound
solutions.body:
Place the targeted dragoon at the origin. A dragoon firing at it has its centre in $[-6,6]^2$, so its square lies inside $[-6.5,6.5]^2$, a square of side $13$ and area $169$. The unit squares have disjoint interiors, so at most $169$ fit, one of which is the target itself: at most $168$ shooters. This is achieved by tiling the $13\times13$ region with unit squares centred at the integer points.

**Answer: 168**

prompt: A zerg player can produce one zergling every minute and a protoss player can produce one zealot every $2.1$ minutes. Both players begin building their respective units immediately from the beginning of the game. In a fight, a zergling army overpowers a zealot army if the ratio of zerglings to zealots is more than $3$. What is the total amount of time (in minutes) during the game such that at that time the zergling army would overpower the zealot army?

solutions.title: Timeline
solutions.body:
At time $t$ there are $\lfloor t\rfloor$ zerglings and $\lfloor t/2.1\rfloor$ zealots; the zerg army overpowers when zerglings $>3\cdot$ zealots.

- From $t=1$ (first zergling) to $t=2.1$ (first zealot) there are zerglings and no zealots: $1.1$ minutes.
- With $k$ zealots (present during $[2.1k,\,2.1(k+1))$) the zerglings must number at least $3k+1$, which happens from $t=3k+1$ on. For $k=1$ this is $t=4$, inside $[2.1,4.2)$: another $0.2$ minutes. For $k\ge2$ we have $3k+1\ge2.1(k+1)$, so the next zealot appears before the zerglings catch up, and the zerg army never overpowers again.

Total: $1.1+0.2=1.3$ minutes.

**Answer: 1.3 minutes**

prompt: There are $111$ StarCraft progamers. The StarCraft team SKT starts with a given set of eleven progamers on it, and at the end of each season, it drops a progamer and adds a progamer (possibly the same one). At the start of the second season, SKT has to field a team of five progamers to play the opening match. How many different lineups of five players could be fielded if the order of players on the lineup matters?

solutions.title: Count unordered teams, then order
solutions.body:
After one season the roster contains at least $10$ of the original $11$ players and at most one new player. A lineup of five uses either no new player: $\binom{11}5=462$ choices; or one new player ($100$ choices of who, since $111-11=100$) and four of the original eleven: $100\cdot\binom{11}4=100\cdot330=33000$ choices. (Each such team is achievable: drop one of the original players not used and add the new one.) Total unordered lineups: $33462$. Order matters, so multiply by $5!=120$: $33462\cdot120=4015440$.

**Answer: 4015440**

prompt: When flipped, a coin has a probability $p$ of landing heads. When flipped twice, it is twice as likely to land on the same side both times as it is to land on each side once. What is the larger possible value of $p$?

solutions.title: Set up the equation
solutions.body:
The probability of the same side twice is $p^2+(1-p)^2=2p^2-2p+1$; of one of each is $2p(1-p)$. The condition is $2p^2-2p+1=2\cdot2p(1-p)=4p-4p^2$, i.e. $6p^2-6p+1=0$, so $p=\frac{3\pm\sqrt3}6$. The larger is $\frac{3+\sqrt3}6$.

**Answer: $\frac{3+\sqrt3}6$**

prompt: George has two coins, one of which is fair and the other of which always comes up heads. Jacob takes one of them at random and flips it twice. Given that it came up heads both times, what is the probability that it is the coin that always comes up heads?

solutions.title: Bayes
solutions.body:
$P(\text{two heads and double-headed})=\frac12\cdot1=\frac12$. $P(\text{two heads})=\frac12\cdot1+\frac12\cdot\frac14=\frac58$. So the conditional probability is $\frac{1/2}{5/8}=\frac45$.

**Answer: $\frac45$**

solutions.title: Compare the two cases
solutions.body:
Before seeing the flips, "double-headed and HH" has probability $\frac12\cdot1=\frac12$ and "fair and HH" has probability $\frac12\cdot\frac14=\frac18$. These are in ratio $4:1$, so given HH the coin is double-headed with probability $\frac45$.

**Answer: $\frac45$**

prompt: Allison has a coin which comes up heads $\frac23$ of the time. She flips it $5$ times. What is the probability that she sees more heads than tails?

solutions.title: Binomial
solutions.body:
More heads than tails means $3,4$ or $5$ heads: $\binom53\left(\frac23\right)^3\left(\frac13\right)^2+\binom54\left(\frac23\right)^4\frac13+\left(\frac23\right)^5=\frac{80+80+32}{243}=\frac{192}{243}=\frac{64}{81}$.

**Answer: $\frac{64}{81}$**

prompt: Newton and Leibniz are playing a game with a coin that comes up heads with probability $p$. They take turns flipping the coin until one of them wins with Newton going first. Newton wins if he flips a heads and Leibniz wins if he flips a tails. Given that Newton and Leibniz each win the game half of the time, what is the probability $p$?

solutions.title: Geometric series
solutions.body:
Newton wins on flip $2n+1$ when the first $2n$ flips alternate in the pattern tails (Newton), heads (Leibniz), repeated $n$ times, and then Newton flips heads: probability $\big((1-p)p\big)^n\,p$. So $P(\text{Newton wins})=\frac{p}{1-p(1-p)}$. Setting this equal to $\frac12$: $2p=1-p+p^2$, so $p^2-3p+1=0$ and $p=\frac{3-\sqrt5}2$ (the other root exceeds $1$).

**Answer: $\frac{3-\sqrt5}{2}$**

solutions.title: Recursive
solutions.body:
Let $N$ be Newton's winning probability. He wins at once with probability $p$. If he flips tails, Leibniz flips: if tails Leibniz wins; if heads (probability $p$) the game restarts. So $N=p+(1-p)p\,N$, giving $N=\frac{p}{1-p+p^2}$ and the same equation as above.

**Answer: $\frac{3-\sqrt5}{2}$**

prompt: Justine has a coin which will come up the same as the last flip $\frac23$ of the time and the other side $\frac13$ of the time. She flips it and it comes up heads. She then flips it $2010$ more times. What is the probability that the last flip is heads?

solutions.title: Parity of changes
solutions.body:
Call a flip a *change* if it differs from the previous flip; each of the $2010$ flips is a change independently with probability $\frac13$. The last flip is heads exactly when the number of changes is even. With $p=\frac23$ (no change) and $q=\frac13$ (change), $P(\text{even})=\frac{(p+q)^{2010}+(p-q)^{2010}}2=\frac{1+(1/3)^{2010}}2$.

So the probability is $\frac{3^{2010}+1}{2\cdot3^{2010}}$.

**Answer: $\dfrac{3^{2010}+1}{2\cdot3^{2010}}$**

solutions.title: Recurrence
solutions.body:
Let $h_n$ be the probability that flip number $n$ is heads, with $h_0=1$. Then $h_{n+1}=\frac23h_n+\frac13(1-h_n)=\frac13h_n+\frac13$, so $h_{n+1}-\frac12=\frac13\left(h_n-\frac12\right)$. Hence $h_{2010}=\frac12+\frac12\cdot3^{-2010}=\frac{3^{2010}+1}{2\cdot3^{2010}}$.

**Answer: $\dfrac{3^{2010}+1}{2\cdot3^{2010}}$**
